title: Technology, Human Rights, Existential Risks & the Information Society
subject: Science, Technology, and Society
description: Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR Articles 1–7), Humans vs. Robots & AI, Nicholas Carr, Bill Joy's GNR existential risks, language, mathematics as nature's language, printing press, World Wide Web, and social media risks.
sourceFile: STS-WK1-MTWThF A book reference in STS.pdf, STS MIDTERM REVIEWER.docx

questions.question: When was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) proclaimed by the UN General Assembly, and how many articles does it contain?
options: December 10, 1948; 30 articles
July 4, 1776; 10 articles
August 15, 2000; 12 articles
June 12, 1898; 50 articles
questions.answer: December 10, 1948; 30 articles
questions.explanation: Crafted after World War II, the UDHR's 30 articles establish inherent human dignity as the foundation of freedom, justice, and peace.

questions.question: Which UDHR Article declares that 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights' and should act in a spirit of brotherhood?
options: Article 1
Article 4
Article 6
Article 7
questions.answer: Article 1
questions.explanation: Articles 1–7 form the 'milestone document': Art 1 (dignity/equality), Art 2 (non-discrimination), Art 3 (life/liberty/security), Art 4 (no slavery), Art 5 (no torture), Art 6 (person before the law), Art 7 (equal protection).

questions.question: According to Chapter 7, what does the good life as a life of justice demand beyond merely identical treatment?
options: Special privileges solely for wealthy tech investors
Preferential treatment and protection for those who have less or are disadvantaged
Eliminating human rights laws for online users
Replacing legal personhood with algorithms
questions.answer: Preferential treatment and protection for those who have less or are disadvantaged
questions.explanation: Human dignity has absolute moral worth and requires uplifting the vulnerable amid rapid technological change.

questions.question: In the Philippines, which major economic sector faces severe job displacement from AI-driven business analytics—with an estimated 1 million Filipino workers potentially affected (Santos, 2017)?
options: Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) industry
Traditional abaca weaving
Cordillera rice farming
Deep-sea pearl diving
questions.answer: Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) industry
questions.explanation: While technology enabled the BPO boom, AI and automated analytics also threaten to displace up to a million BPO workers.

questions.question: What international efforts mentioned in Chapter 7 address the ethical boundaries between humans and robots?
options: South Korean experts crafting ethical guidelines to prevent human-robot exploitation, and European roboticists lobbying for legislation
Banning all calculators worldwide
Replacing judges with humanoid robots in 1948
Granting robots voting rights in the UN
questions.answer: South Korean experts crafting ethical guidelines to prevent human-robot exploitation, and European roboticists lobbying for legislation
questions.explanation: Countries like South Korea and European nations have initiated ethical frameworks as AI and robotics advance.

questions.question: In his 2008 essay 'Is Google Making Us Stupid?', what warning did Nicholas Carr issue about over-relying on search engines and bite-sized digital info?
options: Search engines physically overheat human brains
As we depend on computers to mediate understanding, our own intelligence flattens into artificial intelligence—weakening deep reading and reflection
Google only works in Latin
Machines will stop functioning without paper books
questions.answer: As we depend on computers to mediate understanding, our own intelligence flattens into artificial intelligence—weakening deep reading and reflection
questions.explanation: As machines become more human-like, humans risk acting like mindless automatons swiping for instant answers.

questions.topic: Bill Joy: Why the Future Does Not Need Us
questions.question: Who wrote the controversial 2000 essay 'Why the Future Does Not Need Us,' and what does the acronym GNR stand for?
options: Bill Joy (chief scientist & co-founder/CEO at Sun Microsystems); Genetics, Nanotechnology, and Robotics
Jason Hickel; Global Natural Resources
Tim Berners-Lee; Generalized Network Routing
Freeman Dyson; Geothermal Nuclear Reactors
questions.answer: Bill Joy (chief scientist & co-founder/CEO at Sun Microsystems); Genetics, Nanotechnology, and Robotics
questions.explanation: Bill Joy warned that 21st-century GNR technologies threaten humanity's survival if accepted uncritically.

questions.question: Why does Bill Joy argue that GNR technologies pose a fundamentally different and more dangerous threat than 20th-century nuclear weapons?
options: Because GNR tools cannot be turned off with electricity
Because robots, engineered organisms, and nanobots can self-replicate—one unit can multiply out of control—and are accessible to small groups without massive state facilities
Because nuclear weapons were harmless
Because GNR requires building facilities larger than cities
questions.answer: Because robots, engineered organisms, and nanobots can self-replicate—one unit can multiply out of control—and are accessible to small groups without massive state facilities
questions.explanation: A bomb explodes once, whereas self-replicating GNR systems can multiply exponentially and are far easier for individuals or extremists to abuse.

questions.question: In the documentary 'The Day After Trinity' (1981), what did physicist Freeman Dyson warn overcomes scientists when they feel 'the glitter of nuclear weapons' in their hands?
options: Technical arrogance—an illusion of illimitable power when people see what they can do with their minds
Complete boredom with laboratory work
A desire to return to medieval farming
Fear of basic mathematics
questions.answer: Technical arrogance—an illusion of illimitable power when people see what they can do with their minds
questions.explanation: Paired with J. Robert Oppenheimer's atomic bomb legacy (Hiroshima & Nagasaki, 1945), Dyson warns we must rein in vanity and technical arrogance.

questions.question: Why are words described in Chapter 8 as being 'informed'?
options: Because they are printed exclusively on newspapers
Because they carry 'information'—meaning given by a speaker and intended for a listener, functioning across space and time without losing meaning when multiplied
Because words only exist inside computer hard drives
Because sounds have no structure
questions.answer: Because they carry 'information'—meaning given by a speaker and intended for a listener, functioning across space and time without losing meaning when multiplied
questions.explanation: Words are 'informed' because they carry meaning/information intended by a speaker for a listener.

questions.question: Why can the same spoken or written message be shared with ten, a hundred, or a thousand people without losing its original meaning?
options: Because meaning is not diminished by multiplication—language transmits ideas reliably across space and time
Because sound waves bounce forever without fading
Because only one person is allowed to listen at a time
Because words are made of solid gold
questions.answer: Because meaning is not diminished by multiplication—language transmits ideas reliably across space and time
questions.explanation: Ancient Greeks marveled at how an idea can simultaneously live in both speaker's and listener's minds via language.

questions.question: What does the Greek phrase 'meta phusis' literally mean, and what is Plato's principle of 'One and the Many'?
options: meta phusis: 'after nature'; 'One and the Many': diverse natural beings share an underlying unifying intrinsic nature (illustrated in biology by genus and species)
meta phusis: 'above cities'; 'One and the Many': monopoly economics
meta phusis: 'before dawn'; 'One and the Many': heliocentric orbits
meta phusis: 'within stone'; 'One and the Many': rock gardening
questions.answer: meta phusis: 'after nature'; 'One and the Many': diverse natural beings share an underlying unifying intrinsic nature (illustrated in biology by genus and species)
questions.explanation: Early philosophers sought a unifying factor behind diverse natural phenomena, leading to classification systems like genus and species.

questions.question: According to Chapter 8 (citing Isaac Newton and Eugene Wigner, 1960), what is the 'language of nature' that enables humans to understand natural laws and build modern technology?
options: Cuneiform
Mathematics
Hieroglyphics
Rhetoric
questions.answer: Mathematics
questions.explanation: Nature behaves according to mathematical laws—Newton's great contribution—and human minds can comprehend that mathematical language.

questions.question: Which 1st-century thinker is credited in Chapter 8 with inventing a primitive steam engine long before the Industrial Revolution?
options: Hero of Alexandria
Claudius Ptolemy
Sigmund Freud
Johann Gutenberg
questions.answer: Hero of Alexandria
questions.explanation: Chapter 8 notes Hero of Alexandria built a primitive steam device after conceptually grasping the forces of nature.

questions.question: How did the 15th-century printing press transform Western culture and scientific progress?
options: It kept books locked inside royal tombs
It replaced slow hand-copying, allowed scholars across space and time to share works, and anchored scientific studies in widely accessible books
It eliminated the need for language
It immediately created wireless television
questions.answer: It replaced slow hand-copying, allowed scholars across space and time to share works, and anchored scientific studies in widely accessible books
questions.explanation: Printing fulfilled the Greek ideal of sharing knowledge broadly, accelerating discoveries in electricity, radio, and television.

questions.question: In the modern Information Age (citing Alvin Toffler, 1984), how has the transmission of ideas changed from classical rhetoric?
options: Meaning is conveyed electronically via the digital signal or digit rather than strictly spoken rhetoric
Ideas are carved only on mud tablets
Books are no longer digitized
Radio waves replaced all mathematics
questions.answer: Meaning is conveyed electronically via the digital signal or digit rather than strictly spoken rhetoric
questions.explanation: The digital world is a direct offspring of scientific advances in electricity, magnetism, and computing.

questions.question: Who invented the World Wide Web (alongside Robert Cailliau), at which research organization, and for what immediate scientific need?
options: Sir Tim Berners-Lee at CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research) to process and share massive scientific data from CERN's atom smasher
Bill Joy at Sun Microsystems to sell smartphones
Alan Turing in London to forecast hurricanes
Samuel Kier in Pennsylvania to refine kerosene
questions.answer: Sir Tim Berners-Lee at CERN (European Organization for Nuclear Research) to process and share massive scientific data from CERN's atom smasher
questions.explanation: Berners-Lee used a NeXT computer at CERN as the very first Web server to handle the ocean of particle-accelerator data.

questions.question: What are the major social and ethical risks of today's ease of information sharing on social media?
options: Total lack of internet speed
Disinformation (half-truths/lies), echo chambers reinforcing biases, political manipulation/harassment, and vulnerability to identity theft and online scams
Inability to print paper newspapers
Excessive meditative thinking
questions.answer: Disinformation (half-truths/lies), echo chambers reinforcing biases, political manipulation/harassment, and vulnerability to identity theft and online scams
questions.explanation: Echo chambers limit exposure to clashing ideas, while easy access to personal data requires constant digital vigilance.

questions.question: From which Latin verb does the word 'science' originate, and what does it mean?
options: scire — 'to know'
tekhnē — 'to carve'
klima — 'to slope'
gestell — 'to frame'
questions.answer: scire — 'to know'
questions.explanation: Science derives from the Latin scire ('to know'), reflecting the ancient quest to systematically understand nature.

questions.question: In Chapter 8's activity, what is a 'Caesar cipher' (simple substitution cipher)?
options: A method of encrypting plaintext by shifting or rotating each alphabet letter systematically (e.g., 'I know you' -> 'J lopx zpv' with a left shift of 1)
A Roman stone newspaper engraved in the Forum
A genetic codon table of 64 nucleotides
A type of steam engine valve
questions.answer: A method of encrypting plaintext by shifting or rotating each alphabet letter systematically (e.g., 'I know you' -> 'J lopx zpv' with a left shift of 1)
questions.explanation: Julius Caesar used letter-shift substitution ciphers for private military and political correspondence.

questions.question: Which UDHR protections are guaranteed under Articles 3, 4, and 5 respectively?
options: Art 3: Life, liberty, and security; Art 4: Freedom from slavery/servitude; Art 5: Freedom from torture or cruel/degrading treatment
Art 3: Free internet; Art 4: Patent ownership; Art 5: Free air travel
Art 3: Taxation; Art 4: Military service; Art 5: Voting age
Art 3: Copyright; Art 4: Land ownership; Art 5: Banking privacy
questions.answer: Art 3: Life, liberty, and security; Art 4: Freedom from slavery/servitude; Art 5: Freedom from torture or cruel/degrading treatment
questions.explanation: The first seven UDHR articles safeguard fundamental dignity, liberty, anti-slavery, anti-torture, and legal equality.

questions.question: As AI and humanoid robots become more human-like, what dual ethical dilemma does Chapter 7 highlight?
options: Only battery recycling costs
How to protect human dignity/jobs from replacement and machine errors, AND whether future sentient-like AI would itself require ethical treatment
Whether robots prefer oil or acrylic paint
Whether Google should replace universities
questions.answer: How to protect human dignity/jobs from replacement and machine errors, AND whether future sentient-like AI would itself require ethical treatment
questions.explanation: As machines gain human-like decision-making, society must safeguard both human workers and ethical accountability.

questions.question: During Western periods of warfare and instability before the 15th century, how were ancient words and ideas preserved prior to the printing press?
options: Through manual hand-copying by scribes
Through cloud backups at CERN
Through radio broadcasts
Through photographic film
questions.answer: Through manual hand-copying by scribes
questions.explanation: Manual hand-copying preserved scholarly texts until Gutenberg's printing press enabled global communities of thinkers.

questions.question: Why do scientists continue pursuing Genetics, Nanotechnology, and Robotics despite Bill Joy's warnings?
options: Because GNR promises disease cures, nanomedicine, extended lifespans, and improved quality of life—where small sensible advances accumulate into immense power
Because GNR has no medical applications
Because Joy proved GNR is impossible
Because nuclear weapons were outlawed in 1945
questions.answer: Because GNR promises disease cures, nanomedicine, extended lifespans, and improved quality of life—where small sensible advances accumulate into immense power
questions.explanation: Each incremental step appears beneficial, making it crucial to exercise circumspection and ethical questioning.

questions.question: What critical question opens Chapter 8 ('Information Society') regarding television, smartphones, and the internet?
options: How fast can 5G download movies?
Do modern devices provide genuine information, knowledge, and truth—or merely overwhelming noise?
Which smartphone brand has the brightest screen?
Why did Gutenberg invent the television?
questions.answer: Do modern devices provide genuine information, knowledge, and truth—or merely overwhelming noise?
questions.explanation: Distinguishing truthful, meaningful knowledge from noise and disinformation is the defining challenge of the Information Age.

questions.question: According to Chapter 8, which scientific discoveries directly made the invention of radio and television possible?
options: Discoveries about electricity, magnetism, and electromagnetic waves shared through scholarly publications
Sumerian cuneiform tablets
Mayan floating gardens
Egyptian papyrus ink
questions.answer: Discoveries about electricity, magnetism, and electromagnetic waves shared through scholarly publications
questions.explanation: Scientific knowledge printed and shared across communities fed directly into technological breakthroughs like radio and TV.

questions.question: Why did the ability to name and classify natural objects mark humanity's 'first step toward knowledge'?
options: Because naming and classifying allowed humans to describe, differentiate, and explain things (e.g., how a tree differs from a flower or rock)
Because names generated electricity
Because it eliminated the need for observation
Because it was required by the Roman Senate
questions.answer: Because naming and classifying allowed humans to describe, differentiate, and explain things (e.g., how a tree differs from a flower or rock)
questions.explanation: Language provides the conceptual framework for scientific observation, classification, and shared inquiry.

questions.question: At the close of 'Why the Future Does Not Need Us,' what does Friedrich Nietzsche's line 'The wasteland grows; woe unto him who harbors the wasteland within' warn against?
options: Desert farming techniques
Allowing human arrogance, vanity, and unrestrained technological power to corrupt our inner humanity and destroy the world
Planting trees in urban parks
Studying environmental science
questions.answer: Allowing human arrogance, vanity, and unrestrained technological power to corrupt our inner humanity and destroy the world
questions.explanation: Ethical restraint and inner moral grounding must match our growing scientific power.

questions.question: What rights are protected by Articles 6 and 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
options: Art 6: Recognition everywhere as a person before the law; Art 7: Equality before the law and equal protection against discrimination
Art 6: Right to free smartphones; Art 7: Right to own patents
Art 6: Right to free travel; Art 7: Right to tax exemption
Art 6: Right to silence; Art 7: Right to privacy only for corporations
questions.answer: Art 6: Recognition everywhere as a person before the law; Art 7: Equality before the law and equal protection against discrimination
questions.explanation: Articles 6 and 7 ensure universal legal standing and non-discriminatory protection under the law.

questions.question: What core civic duty does Chapter 8 emphasize for citizens navigating modern information technologies?
options: Disconnect permanently from all electricity
Remain vigilant against scams/identity theft, verify truth against disinformation, and use technology responsibly without harming others or ourselves
Share every unverified rumor immediately
Ignore privacy settings completely
questions.answer: Remain vigilant against scams/identity theft, verify truth against disinformation, and use technology responsibly without harming others or ourselves
questions.explanation: From ancient sails to the World Wide Web, technology requires ethical responsibility alongside curiosity.
